questions.stem: How many chromosomes does a human gamete carry?

options.text: 23, half the number in body cells
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
46 is the diploid body-cell number; gametes halve it.
Nothing doubles to 92 at meiosis.
Gametes hold 23 singles, not 23 pairs.

questions.stem: Which adaptation helps a sperm cell reach the ovum?

options.text: Cilia that sweep it down the oviduct
options.explanation: Cilia line the oviduct wall; the sperm swims itself.

options.text: A tail that propels it, powered by mitochondria
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: A thick energy store in its cytoplasm
options.explanation: Energy stores belong to the egg cell.

options.text: A hard coat that blocks rivals
options.explanation: No taught sperm coat blocks rivals.

questions.stem: Why does the ovum carry energy stores in its cytoplasm?

options.explanation: The sperm brings its own mitochondria.
Lining growth is hormonal, not cytoplasmic.

options.text: To support the early embryo's development before other nutrition arrives
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
The ovum does not swim.

questions.stem: Which cells are produced by meiosis?

options.explanation: Body cells divide by mitosis.
The zygote divides by mitosis, not meiosis.

options.text: The cells of the uterine lining
options.explanation: Lining cells are ordinary diploid body cells.

options.text: The gametes — sperm and ovum in animals, pollen nucleus and ovum in plants
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

questions.stem: A lab images two cells: one tiny with a long tail, one large with dense cytoplasm. What has been photographed?

options.text: A sperm and an ovum — the two human gametes
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Body cells show neither tails nor gamete cytoplasm.
A zygote has fused nuclei and no tail.

options.text: A pollen grain and a seed
options.explanation: Seeds and pollen are plant structures, not human cells.

questions.stem: State the chromosome number in a human gamete and say how it compares with body cells.
questions.modelAnswer: A human gamete carries 23 chromosomes, half the number found in normal body cells.

questions.stem: Name the two adaptations of a sperm cell mentioned in the lesson.
questions.modelAnswer: A sperm has a tail to propel it and mitochondria to provide energy for that movement.

questions.stem: Explain why gametes must be produced by meiosis rather than mitosis.
questions.modelAnswer: Meiosis halves the chromosome number so that fertilisation restores the full count; mitotic gametes would produce a zygote with double the normal chromosomes.

questions.stem: A new fertility treatment selects sperm with the strongest swimming. Name the structure being assessed and its energy supplier.
questions.modelAnswer: The structure assessed is the tail, and its movement is powered by mitochondria supplying energy.

options.text: The growth of the uterine lining
options.explanation: Lining growth prepares implantation, not fusion.

options.text: The fusion of a male gamete and a female gamete to produce a zygote
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: The division of a zygote into an embryo
options.explanation: That follows fertilisation; it is not fertilisation itself.

options.text: The release of an egg from the ovary
options.explanation: That is ovulation.

questions.stem: Where in the human female does fertilisation usually happen?

options.explanation: The ovary releases the egg but does not host fertilisation.
Sperm are deposited near the vagina's top; fusion happens higher up.
Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
The uterus hosts implantation; the oviduct hosts fusion.

questions.stem: How many chromosomes does a human zygote hold, and from where?

options.explanation: 23 is the gamete count; the zygote restores 46.
Both parents contribute half each.
Fusion adds 23 to 23, not doubles 46.

options.text: 46 — half from the father and half from the mother
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

questions.stem: Which type of cell division turns the zygote into a many-celled embryo?

options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Meiosis made the gametes; it does not grow the embryo.
Fusion is the fertilisation event, not a division.
Specialisation follows; the copying division is mitosis.

questions.stem: After fertilisation, some zygote descendant cells become muscle while others become nerve. What happened?

options.explanation: All descendant cells keep the same 46.

options.text: The cells specialised to perform specific functions during embryo development
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Meiosis does not run in the embryo's tissues.

options.text: The cells fused with new gametes
options.explanation: No further gametes join the embryo.

questions.stem: State the event that occurs in the oviduct one to two days after ovulation if sperm are present.
questions.modelAnswer: Fertilisation occurs in the oviduct when a sperm meets the egg, typically one to two days after ovulation.

questions.stem: State what a zygote divides by and what it develops into.
questions.modelAnswer: The zygote divides by mitosis and develops into an embryo.

questions.stem: Explain why a zygote contains 46 chromosomes when each gamete contained only 23.
questions.modelAnswer: Fertilisation fuses two gametes, so the 23 chromosomes from the sperm and the 23 from the egg combine to give the full 46.

questions.stem: A couple conceive naturally. State the chromosome source split in their child's body cells.
questions.modelAnswer: Every body cell carries 46 chromosomes, with 23 inherited from the father and 23 from the mother.
